before.content_html:
Factors Influencing Metal Selection

Choosing the right metal for a product is rarely straightforward. Designers must balance a range of sometimes competing factors to arrive at the most appropriate choice. No single property determines the decision — a metal that is mechanically perfect may be too expensive, too heavy or impossible to source in the required stock form.

The principal factors are:

  • Function — the mechanical demands placed on the product. A bridge cable must have very high tensile strength; a cooking pot must conduct heat efficiently and resist corrosion from food acids. The function defines which properties are non-negotiable.
  • Cost — raw material cost, ease of machining and finishing all affect the final product cost. Mild steel is cheap and easy to process; titanium offers outstanding strength-to-weight ratio but costs approximately 50 times more per kilogram.
  • Aesthetics — appearance matters for consumer products. Copper has a warm, distinctive colour and develops a patina; polished stainless steel projects a modern, hygienic image. Anodised aluminium can be given vivid colours for consumer electronics and sporting equipment.
  • Availability — even the ideal metal is useless if it cannot be sourced in the required quantity, lead time or stock form. Exotic alloys may only be available from specialist suppliers with long lead times, disrupting production schedules.
  • Environment — the operating environment determines corrosion resistance requirements. A boat hull operates in salt water; a storage rack in a dry warehouse faces very different corrosion risks. Materials used in food contact must comply with food-safety regulations.
Key Fact

A complete metal-selection answer must address at least two factors: the key functional property (e.g. tensile strength, corrosion resistance) and one additional factor (cost, availability, aesthetics or environment). Answers that only cite one property will not reach the higher mark bands at Eduqas.

Stock Forms

Metals are supplied commercially in a range of stock forms. Selecting the appropriate stock form reduces the amount of material that must be removed and can simplify manufacturing. Common metal stock forms include:

  • Sheet and plate — flat, rolled metal. Sheet is typically under 3 mm thick; plate is 3 mm and above. Used for car body panels (sheet steel), structural decking (plate steel) and roofing (copper sheet).
  • Bar and rod — solid sections with circular, square, hexagonal or rectangular cross-sections. Hexagonal bar is used for nuts and bolt blanks; round bar is turned on a lathe to produce shafts and spindles.
  • Tube — hollow cylindrical or square section. Used in bicycle frames (lightweight tubing), handrails and scaffolding. The hollow section gives a high strength-to-weight ratio.
  • Angle section — L-shaped cross-section, used in shelving frameworks, brackets and structural frames. Provides rigidity without excessive weight.

Selecting the most appropriate stock form from the outset saves significant machining time and reduces material waste. If a component is essentially a hollow cylinder (such as a handrail or a bicycle fork), starting from tube rather than solid rod eliminates the need to bore out the centre — a time-consuming and wasteful operation. Similarly, using angle section for shelf brackets means the required L-shaped profile already exists; cutting it from flat plate would waste roughly half the material. Designers should always ask which stock form most closely matches the final component geometry before choosing a process.

Forces, Stresses and Work Hardening

When metals are in service they experience various forces. Understanding these helps designers choose the right metal and design to minimise failure:

  • Tension — a stretching force pulling the material apart (e.g. a lifting cable). Requires high tensile strength.
  • Compression — a squashing force (e.g. a column supporting a load). Cast iron performs well in compression.
  • Shear — forces acting in opposite directions across a cross-section (e.g. the force on a rivet holding two plates together).
  • Torsion — a twisting force (e.g. a drive shaft transmitting rotary motion from an engine to the wheels).

Work hardening occurs when a metal is repeatedly deformed at room temperature. Each deformation increases the dislocation density in the metal’s crystal structure, making it harder but less ductile. A paperclip repeatedly bent back and forth becomes harder and eventually snaps — this is work hardening in action. It can be useful (cold-drawing wire to increase its strength) or problematic (a sheet of metal becoming too brittle to bend further during forming).

The mechanical properties of steel are not fixed; they can be deliberately altered by carefully controlled heating and cooling. This is because the crystal structure of iron changes at specific temperatures. By controlling the temperature and the rate of cooling, engineers can produce steels ranging from very soft and ductile (for forming) to extremely hard (for cutting tools). Heat treatment therefore gives designers a second layer of material selection: not just which steel to use, but which state to use it in.

Heat treatment processes are most commonly applied to carbon steels and high-speed steels. They are generally not used for mild steel (too little carbon to respond significantly) and cannot make non-ferrous metals such as aluminium hard in the same way, though aluminium alloys can be heat-treated to improve strength by a different mechanism (precipitation hardening).

Heat Treatment Processes

The main heat treatment processes for steel are annealing, hardening, tempering, normalising and case hardening. Each involves different temperatures and cooling rates, producing different outcomes:

  • Annealing — the steel is heated to a specific temperature (typically 700–900 °C depending on carbon content), held there to allow the crystal structure to reorganise, then cooled very slowly (usually by leaving it in the furnace to cool). The result is a soft, ductile metal that is easy to machine or form. Annealing is used to relieve internal stresses after welding or to restore ductility to work-hardened metal.
  • Hardening — the steel is heated above its critical temperature (typically 760–900 °C) until it glows orange/yellow, then quenched (plunged rapidly into water, oil or brine). The rapid cooling prevents the carbon atoms from migrating, locking a hard but brittle crystal structure (martensite) in place. The steel is now very hard but too brittle for most uses and must be tempered.
  • Tempering — always follows hardening. The hardened steel is reheated to a lower temperature (150–400 °C, depending on the required toughness), held briefly, then allowed to cool in air. This reduces some of the brittleness introduced by hardening while retaining most of the hardness. The temperature is judged by oxide colours that appear on polished steel: pale yellow (∼220 °C) for scrapers, blue (∼300 °C) for springs. Tempering produces a balance of hardness and toughness.
  • Normalising — similar to annealing but the steel is cooled in still air rather than in the furnace. This produces a slightly harder and stronger result than full annealing. Normalising is used to refine the grain structure after forging or hot rolling, producing a more uniform microstructure across the material.
  • Case hardening — used specifically for mild steel, which has too little carbon to be hardened by quenching alone. The surface is enriched with carbon (by heating in a carbon-rich medium such as charcoal powder) and then quenched. The result is a hard outer case with a tough, ductile core. This combination is ideal for gear teeth and camshafts, which need a wear-resistant surface but a core that can absorb impact without shattering.
Key Fact

Hardening makes steel very hard but brittle; it is always followed by tempering to restore some toughness. Annealing (furnace cool) produces the softest result; normalising (air cool) gives a slightly stronger outcome. Case hardening applies only to mild steel and produces a hard surface over a tough core.

practice_questions.text:
Which heat treatment process produces the softest, most ductile result in steel?
A) Hardening
B) Tempering
C) Annealing
D) Case hardening
Name two stock forms in which aluminium sheet metal is commercially supplied.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: sheet / plate / bar / rod / tube / angle section. Must be standard stock forms. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to mild steel during work hardening.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• When mild steel is repeatedly bent or cold-worked, dislocations build up in its crystal structure.
• This makes the metal progressively harder.
• However, the metal also becomes less ductile (more brittle) and will eventually crack or fracture if deformation continues. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the hardening process must always be followed by tempering.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hardening (heating then rapid quenching) produces a very hard but extremely brittle crystal structure in the steel.
• A hardened but untempered steel would fracture under impact or shock loading, making it unsuitable for most applications.
• Tempering reheats the hardened steel to a lower temperature (150-400°C), which relieves internal stresses and allows some ductility to return.
• The result is a steel that retains much of its hardness while gaining enough toughness to withstand the forces in service, e.g. a chisel blade that cuts without shattering.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why case hardening is used for the gear teeth of a bicycle gearbox rather than simply using high carbon steel throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Gear teeth need a very hard, wear-resistant surface to withstand repeated metal-to-metal contact without deteriorating.
• The core of the gear must be tough enough to absorb the shock loads transmitted by rapid gear changes without fracturing.
• High carbon steel throughout would be hard but brittle: the entire gear, including the root of each tooth, would be at risk of sudden fracture under impact.
• Case hardening on mild steel addresses both requirements: the surface is enriched with carbon and quenched to produce a hard case, while the mild steel core remains tough and ductile.
• This combination extends product life and improves safety compared to a uniformly hard but brittle gear.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both surface and core requirements explained, mechanism of case hardening described, compared to alternative with reference to product context. Secure: Both requirements and the process described but comparison limited. Developing: Process described but link to product requirements thin. Emerging: Superficial reference to hardening without explaining the case/core distinction.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using titanium rather than mild steel for the frame of a high-performance bicycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of titanium:
• Titanium has an exceptional strength-to-weight ratio; a titanium frame can be as strong as steel at a fraction of the mass, reducing overall bicycle weight and improving performance.
• Titanium is highly corrosion resistant without any surface treatment, making it suitable for use in wet, muddy and salty conditions without rusting.
• Titanium has a degree of flex that can provide a more comfortable ride than the stiffer steel alternative.
• Long service life means less frequent replacement; over a lifetime the higher initial cost may be offset.
Disadvantages of titanium:
• Titanium costs approximately 50 times more per kilogram than mild steel, making titanium frames prohibitively expensive for most consumers.
• Titanium is significantly more difficult to machine and weld; it must be welded in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, requiring specialist equipment and skilled labour, further increasing cost.
• Titanium is less readily available than mild steel, making repairs in the field or by a local welder less practical.
• Mild steel frames can be easily repaired, reshaped and sourced cheaply; this is a significant advantage for budget and touring cyclists.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, linked to bicycle performance and manufacturing context. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; limited balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]

before.content_html:
Categories of Shaping Processes

Metal shaping processes are grouped by whether they remove material, deform it without removing any, or reform it from a liquid or granular state. Understanding these categories helps you select the most efficient process for a given product and scale of production. The three main categories are wastage (material is removed), deforming/reforming (material is reshaped without significant removal) and fabricating (joining, covered in Lesson 4).

Marking Out

Before any cutting or shaping can begin, the metal must be marked out accurately. Marking out transfers measurements and cutting lines onto the metal surface. Key tools include:

  • Engineer’s blue (layout fluid) — a dye applied to the metal surface so that scribed lines are clearly visible against the dark background.
  • Scriber — a hardened steel tool used to scratch a fine line into the metal surface, following a rule or template.
  • Centre punch — used with a hammer to mark the exact centre of a hole before drilling; the indent prevents the drill bit from wandering at the start of the cut.
  • Engineer’s square — ensures lines are scribed at exactly 90° to a datum edge, critical for accurate right-angle cuts.
  • Vernier calliper — a precision measuring instrument capable of measuring internal and external dimensions to 0.02 mm; essential for close-tolerance engineering work.

Wastage Processes

Wastage processes remove material to achieve the desired shape. They are also called subtractive processes. The material removed (swarf, off-cuts) is waste that must be managed and, ideally, recycled. Common wastage processes for metals include:

  • Sawing — hand hacksaw or powered bandsaw used to cut metal to length or cut out profiles. A hacksaw blade should have at least two teeth in contact with thin material at all times to prevent the blade snagging.
  • Filing — removes small amounts of material to achieve a smooth surface or a precise fit. Files are classified by their cut (single-cut, double-cut, rasp) and their coarseness (rough, bastard, second-cut, smooth). Always use a file handle to prevent injury from the tang.
  • Drilling — a rotating drill bit removes material to form a cylindrical hole. The centre punch indent ensures accurate positioning. A pillar drill (bench drill) provides more accurate and safer drilling than a hand-held drill, with depth stops to control hole depth.
  • Milling — a rotating multi-tooth cutter moves across the workpiece surface to remove material and create flat faces, slots or profiles. A vertical milling machine allows precise three-axis movement (X, Y, Z). CNC milling machines are programmable and used for high-volume, complex components.
  • Turning (lathe work) — the workpiece rotates against a stationary cutting tool. A centre lathe can produce cylindrical shapes (shafts, pins), taper sections and threaded forms. Operations on a lathe include rough turning, facing (flattening the end), parting off (cutting to length) and thread cutting.
  • Laser cutting — a high-powered laser beam melts and vaporises metal along a precise path controlled by a computer. Produces extremely accurate cuts with minimal kerf width and little heat-affected zone in thin sheet metal. Suitable for intricate profiles that would be impossible or very slow with mechanical cutting.
  • Plasma cutting — a jet of ionised gas (plasma) at temperatures exceeding 20,000 °C melts through thicker plate steel. Faster and cheaper than laser cutting for thick material, but with a wider kerf and rougher edge finish. Widely used in shipbuilding and structural steelwork.
Key Fact

On a lathe, the workpiece rotates and the cutting tool is stationary. On a milling machine, the cutter rotates and the workpiece is moved. Confusing these two is a common error in GCSE answers describing machining operations.

Casting

Casting processes involve pouring or injecting molten metal into a mould where it solidifies into the desired shape. They can produce complex three-dimensional forms that would be very difficult to achieve by machining. The two main casting methods at GCSE are:

  • Sand casting — a pattern (often made from wood or metal) is pressed into compacted sand to form a cavity. The pattern is removed and molten metal is poured in through a runner. After cooling, the sand mould is broken apart and the casting removed. Sand casting is relatively low-cost but produces a rough surface finish that usually requires machining. It is suitable for one-off and low-volume production and can produce very large castings (e.g. engine blocks, manhole covers).
  • Die casting — molten metal is forced under high pressure into a reusable steel die. The die produces castings with a smooth surface finish and high dimensional accuracy. Die casting is suited to high-volume production of small-to-medium components in low-melting-point non-ferrous metals (zinc, aluminium, lead alloys). Examples include carburettor bodies, toy car shells and electrical connector housings.

Deforming and Reforming

Deforming processes reshape metal without removing material, using compressive or tensile forces. They are efficient because almost no material is wasted:

  • Forging — a heated billet of metal is shaped by compressive forces, applied by hammering (drop forging) or squeezing (press forging) between shaped dies. Forging aligns the grain structure of the metal along the profile of the component, producing excellent strength and fatigue resistance. Car crankshafts, spanners and connecting rods are forged because the aligned grain makes them stronger than equivalent castings.
  • Press forming (pressing) — sheet metal is placed between a punch (male die) and a die (female die); the punch descends under hydraulic pressure and forces the sheet into the die cavity. Used for very high-volume production of identical parts: car body panels, sinks and baking tins are all press-formed. The process is extremely fast once tooling is set up.
  • Bending — metal sheet or bar is bent over a former or in a folder (pan brake) to produce angled or curved forms. A sheet metal folder uses a clamping beam and a folding beam to produce clean, accurate bends without thinning the material excessively. Simple, low-cost process suitable for one-off and batch work.

Sand casting uses a disposable mould broken after each casting; tooling costs are low and very large or complex components can be produced, but surface finish is rough and dimensional accuracy is limited. Die casting uses an expensive reusable steel die; tooling costs are very high (£10,000–£100,000+), but once the die is made, parts are produced rapidly with excellent surface finish and close tolerances. Die casting is therefore only economical for high-volume production (tens of thousands of parts) where the tooling cost is spread over many units. For a one-off or prototype, sand casting (or CNC machining from solid) is far more practical.

An important limitation of die casting is that the steel die cannot withstand the very high temperatures of ferrous metals such as steel; die casting is therefore restricted to lower-melting-point non-ferrous alloys. Sand casting can be used with virtually any metal, including cast iron and steel.

Forging is preferred over casting whenever a component must withstand repeated impact, bending or fatigue loading during its service life. Forging aligns the metal’s grain structure along the profile of the part, so the strongest direction of the grain runs through the sections that must resist the greatest forces — this is why car crankshafts and connecting rods are always forged rather than cast. Casting is better suited to components with complex internal cavities or very large cross-sections where forging dies would be impractical to make or too expensive for the production volume.

Key Fact

Forging produces a stronger component than casting for the same shape because the forging process aligns the metal’s grain structure along the profile of the component. A forged spanner is stronger than a cast one because its grain follows the shape of the jaws, resisting the bending forces applied in use.

Categories of Metal Joining

Metal components are joined either permanently (the joint is intended to be inseparable without destroying the parts) or temporarily (the joint can be disassembled and reassembled). Selecting the right joining method depends on the metals involved, the forces the joint must withstand, whether disassembly is needed for maintenance, and the required production speed.

Welding

Welding is the strongest permanent joining process for metals. It works by melting the parent (base) metal at the joint and, usually, adding a filler rod of similar composition. On cooling, the metals fuse into a single homogeneous joint. The three main arc-based welding processes are:

  • MIG welding (Metal Inert Gas) — a consumable wire electrode is automatically fed through the welding gun while a shielding gas (pure argon is inert for true MIG; an argon/CO&sub2; mix makes it MAG welding) protects the molten pool from atmospheric contamination. MIG is fast, easy to learn and suitable for steel and aluminium; widely used in automotive and general fabrication.
  • TIG welding (Tungsten Inert Gas) — a non-consumable tungsten electrode creates the arc; filler rod is added separately by hand. TIG produces a very clean, precise weld bead with excellent control over heat input. It is used for thin sheet, stainless steel, aluminium and titanium where weld quality is critical (aerospace, food equipment, artistic metalwork). TIG is slower and requires greater skill than MIG.
  • Arc welding (MMA — Manual Metal Arc) — a flux-coated electrode is used; the flux melts and forms a protective slag over the weld pool, eliminating the need for shielding gas. Simpler and cheaper equipment; suitable for outdoor use and for joining thick or rusty steel. The weld quality is generally lower than MIG or TIG and the slag must be chipped away after welding.
Key Fact

In welding, the base metal melts and fuses with a filler of the same composition — the joint becomes part of the parent material. In brazing and soldering, the base metal does NOT melt; only a lower-melting-point filler is melted and drawn into the joint by capillary action. Brazing uses filler melting above 450 °C; soldering uses filler melting below 450 °C.

Brazing and Soldering

Brazing uses a brass-based or silver-based filler alloy with a melting point above 450 °C (typically 700–900 °C). A flux is applied to prevent oxidation. The base metals are heated with an oxy-acetylene or propane torch until the filler melts and flows into the joint by capillary action. The joint is strong, neat and suitable for copper alloys and dissimilar metals. Brazed joints on copper pipe work and cycle frame lugs are common examples.

Soldering uses a tin-based filler alloy melting below 450 °C (soft solder melts at around 180–190 °C). It is used where low heat input is essential — electronic circuit boards (where high heat would destroy components), copper plumbing joints and jewellery. Flux is applied to clean the joint surfaces. Soldered joints are much weaker than brazed or welded joints and are not suitable where mechanical strength is the primary requirement. The critical difference from brazing is the lower temperature: in soldering the base metal remains entirely solid.

Riveting

Riveting is a permanent mechanical fastening method. A rivet is a short cylindrical pin with a preformed head. The plain (tail) end passes through pre-drilled holes in the parts being joined and is then deformed to form a second head, clamping the parts together. Riveting does not require heat and can join dissimilar metals. Pop rivets (blind rivets) can be set from one side only using a rivet gun; the mandrel is pulled through the rivet body, expanding the tail inside the joint, then snaps off. Pop rivets are widely used in aircraft skins, guttering and sheet metal enclosures. Traditional solid rivets (used in structural steelwork and older aircraft) require access to both sides and are stronger but slower to set.

Temporary Joining

Temporary joints can be disassembled without destroying either component. They are used wherever maintenance, adjustment or replacement of parts is required:

  • Nuts and bolts — the bolt passes through clearance holes in both parts; a nut is tightened onto the threaded end. Can be locked against loosening by a lock nut, spring washer or thread-locking adhesive. Suitable for heavy-duty structural joints (machinery, motor vehicle components).
  • Machine screws — similar to bolts but thread directly into a tapped (threaded) hole in one of the components, or into a threaded insert. Used in precision assemblies, electronics enclosures and consumer products where a clean appearance is needed (countersunk machine screws sit flush with the surface).
  • Self-tapping screws — cut their own thread as they are driven into a pre-drilled pilot hole; used for joining thin sheet metal without the need for a separate nut.

The choice between nuts and bolts, machine screws and self-tapping screws depends on the forces involved, the thickness of the material and whether a nut or tapped hole is feasible. Nuts and bolts provide the highest clamping force and can be torqued to a precise specification, making them suitable for safety-critical structural joints such as engine mountings. Machine screws suit precision enclosures where a flush appearance matters and the wall thickness allows tapping. Self-tapping screws offer the fastest assembly in thin sheet metal because no nut or separate tapping operation is needed.

The three thermal joining processes are frequently confused. The key distinguishing variable is whether the parent metal melts. In welding (MIG, TIG, arc) the parent metal reaches its melting point and the filler is the same or similar alloy; the cooled joint is essentially continuous with the parent material. In brazing the parent does not melt (it is kept below its melting point); the filler (brass or silver alloy, above 450 °C) flows into the gap by capillary action and bonds metallurgically. In soldering the parent again does not melt; the filler (tin-based, below 450 °C) flows in by capillary action and bonds by adhesion and limited diffusion. Joint strength decreases in the sequence welding > brazing > soldering.

Temperature comparison: arc welding steel reaches approximately 3,500 °C at the arc; brazing with a propane torch might heat the joint to 750 °C; soldering a circuit board operates at around 250 °C. These temperature differences explain why soldering is safe for delicate electronic components but welding would destroy them instantly.

Surface Finishes and Corrosion Protection

Most ferrous metals corrode when exposed to moisture and oxygen; many non-ferrous metals also deteriorate in certain environments. Surface finishes serve two main purposes: protecting the metal from corrosion and improving its appearance. Common surface treatments include:

  • Painting — the simplest and most versatile finish. A primer is applied first to improve adhesion and provide an initial corrosion barrier; topcoat paint provides colour and further protection. Breaks in the paint film expose the metal to corrosion, so surface preparation (cleaning, degreasing, sanding or shot-blasting) is critical for paint adhesion.
  • Powder coating — dry polymer powder is electrostatically applied to the metal surface and then cured in an oven at 180–200 °C, fusing into a tough, uniform film. Provides better impact resistance, corrosion resistance and consistency of finish than liquid paint. Used on bicycle frames, garden furniture and electrical enclosures.
  • Electroplating — a thin layer of a corrosion-resistant or decorative metal (chrome, nickel, zinc, gold) is deposited onto the base metal using an electrolytic process. Chromium plating on taps and car trim provides a bright, hard, corrosion-resistant surface; zinc electroplating (electro-galvanising) provides sacrificial protection to steel.
  • Anodising — an electrochemical process specific to aluminium. The aluminium is made the anode in an electrolytic bath; this thickens the natural oxide layer on the surface, greatly improving corrosion and abrasion resistance. The porous anodised layer can be dyed in a wide range of colours before sealing. Used on bicycle components, laptop cases and sporting equipment.
  • Galvanising — steel is dipped in molten zinc (hot-dip galvanising), coating it with a tough zinc layer. The zinc provides both a physical barrier and sacrificial protection: zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes preferentially if the coating is damaged, protecting the underlying steel. Used on fence posts, crash barriers, steel road signs and structural steelwork.
  • Dip coating (plastic dip coating) — the metal is preheated and dipped into a tank of powdered or liquid thermoplastic (often PVC or polyethylene). The plastic melts onto the surface and solidifies as a thick, flexible, grip-able coating. Used on tool handles, garden tools, dishwasher baskets and wire shelving. Provides excellent grip, insulation and corrosion protection.
  • Polishing — progressive abrasion using finer and finer abrasives, finishing with a buffing compound, produces a mirror-like surface on metals such as stainless steel, aluminium and copper. Used for decorative products (trophies, jewellery, cookware). Polishing is a surface preparation, not a corrosion barrier — a polished surface must still be lacquered or otherwise protected if corrosion resistance is required.
Key Fact

Galvanising applies to steel and uses a zinc coating that provides sacrificial protection (the zinc corrodes first). Anodising applies only to aluminium and is an electrochemical process that thickens the existing oxide layer; it does not involve a separate metal coating. Confusing the two is a frequent exam error.

Scales of Production

The scale at which a metal product is manufactured fundamentally affects the choice of materials, processes, tooling and cost. There are four main scales of production, each suited to a different volume and context:

  • One-off (bespoke) production — a single unique item made to individual specification. Examples include a commissioned sculpture, a prototype aircraft component or a replacement machine part. Highly skilled labour is required; unit cost is high because no tooling investment is spread over multiple units. Processes: hand fabrication, one-off sand casting, manual TIG welding.
  • Batch production — a set number of identical products made together, then production switches to another product. Between batches, machines are reset and tooling is changed. Examples include a run of 500 steel brackets for a construction project, or a seasonal run of cast iron cookware. Tooling costs are shared across the batch, reducing unit cost compared to one-off. Processes: CNC machining, press forming, sand casting.
  • Mass production — high volumes of a standardised product manufactured continuously on dedicated production lines with purpose-built tooling. Examples include car body panels (press formed from mild steel sheet), aluminium drink cans (drawn and ironed from aluminium sheet) and steel nails. Unit cost is very low because tooling cost is spread over millions of units; however, the high capital investment in tooling and machinery means mass production is only viable for products with very high demand. Die casting and automated MIG welding are typical mass production processes for metals.
  • Continuous production — the process runs without interruption, 24 hours a day. Used for primary metal production processes such as steel rolling (producing coils of sheet steel), wire drawing (copper wire for cables) and aluminium extrusion. The product is not a discrete item but a continuous form (coil, wire, extruded section) that is cut to length at the point of use.
Key Fact

The higher the production volume, the lower the unit cost — but only once the initial tooling investment has been recovered. A die casting die can cost £50,000 or more; at 10 units this is unaffordable, but at 100,000 units it adds only £0.50 per part. This is why mass production requires high demand to be economically viable.

Sustainability and the 6Rs for Metals

Metal products have significant sustainability implications across their full lifecycle — from ore extraction to manufacture, use and end of life. The 6Rs framework (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Reclaim, Repair and Rethink) provides a structured way to evaluate and improve the sustainability of metal products:

  • Reduce — use less material in the first place. Structural optimisation (topology optimisation, for example) removes material from metal components in low-stress regions, reducing the mass of a part by 30–50% without compromising strength. Reducing material use also reduces energy consumed in production and transport.
  • Reuse — use the same product or component again without reprocessing. Steel structural beams from demolished buildings are routinely reused in new construction. Refillable aluminium gas cylinders are another example.
  • Recycle — metals are among the most recyclable materials. Steel is the world’s most recycled material by mass; around 86% of steel used in the UK is recycled. Recycled steel uses approximately 74% less energy than virgin steel from iron ore. Recycled aluminium uses only approximately 5% of the energy of primary smelting from bauxite. Effective recycling requires separation of metal types; mixed metal scrap has lower value and reduced recyclability.
  • Reclaim — recover material that would otherwise be wasted. Swarf and off-cuts from machining operations are collected and returned to smelters. Precious metals such as gold and silver are recovered from waste electronic equipment (e-waste) through urban mining.
  • Repair — extend the service life of a metal product through maintenance. Welding cracked or worn components, re-coating corroded surfaces (re-painting, re-galvanising) and replacing individual worn parts delays the need for a complete replacement and reduces total resource consumption.
  • Rethink — fundamentally reconsider whether the product is designed for sustainability. Is the metal product designed for disassembly? Are fasteners accessible for recycling separation? Can dissimilar metals bonded together be separated? Could a lighter or more readily recyclable metal be substituted? Rethinking often produces the largest sustainability gains.

All primary metal comes from ore — a finite, non-renewable resource formed over geological timescales. Some metals face genuine supply concerns: indium (used in LCD screens) and gallium (used in solar cells and semiconductors) have projected reserves of only a few decades at current extraction rates. Even common metals such as copper have ore grades declining over time as the highest-concentration deposits are exhausted, meaning more rock must be processed per tonne of copper recovered, increasing energy use and waste rock volumes. This makes recycling not just an environmental preference but an economic and strategic necessity for modern manufacturing.

The concept of a circular economy applies directly to metals: rather than a linear “extract → make → dispose” model, a circular economy keeps metals in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling, and designs products from the outset for easy disassembly and material recovery.

Case Study: The Aluminium Drink Can

The aluminium beverage can is one of the most successful examples of metal product design and sustainable manufacturing. Each can is produced by the drawing and ironing (D&I) process: a circular blank is stamped from a coil of aluminium alloy (typically AA3104 — an alloy of aluminium, manganese and magnesium), deep-drawn into a cup, then ironed through a series of rings to reduce the wall thickness to approximately 0.097 mm while stretching the can to its full height. The base is domed inward to resist the internal pressure of carbonated drinks.

The can is designed for structural efficiency: the thin wall is strong enough because the internal pressure of the contents stiffens it (pressurised vessel effect). The domed base enables the can to withstand approximately 90 psi of internal pressure. Mass production rates exceed 2,000 cans per minute on a single production line, demonstrating how continuous and mass production methods make a seemingly simple metal product one of the most precisely engineered items in everyday life.

From a sustainability perspective, aluminium is highly suitable: UK aluminium can recycling rates exceed 70%, and a recycled can is back on the shelf within 60 days of disposal. The energy saving of approximately 95% per recycled can compared to virgin aluminium makes the recycling system economically as well as environmentally advantageous.

Smart Alloys and Shape Memory Alloys

Shape memory alloys (SMAs) are a class of smart material that can be deformed at a lower temperature and then recover their original shape when heated to their specific transformation temperature. The most commercially important SMA is nitinol (nickel-titanium alloy, named after its composition and the Naval Ordnance Laboratory where it was discovered). Nitinol has a transformation temperature that can be engineered between −100 °C and +100 °C depending on the exact alloy composition.

Applications of shape memory alloys include:

  • Medical stents — a nitinol stent is cooled and crimped onto a catheter, inserted into a blocked artery, and then released into the warm body where it expands to its pre-set open shape, propping the artery open. No mechanical inflation device is needed.
  • Orthodontic arch wires — nitinol wire applies a continuous, gentle force to teeth as it tries to return to its straight pre-set shape at body temperature, moving teeth more effectively and comfortably than conventional stainless steel wires.
  • Actuators in engineering — SMA wires can replace small electric motors or solenoids to open valves, release latches or actuate mechanisms in response to temperature change, useful in aerospace and robotics where weight and space are at a premium.
  • Eyeglass frames — nitinol frames can be bent significantly without permanently deforming, then spring back to shape — a practical version of the shape memory effect at room temperature (superelasticity).
Key Fact

Shape memory alloys (SMAs) are classified as smart materials because they respond to an external stimulus (temperature) in a controlled, predictable way. Unlike conventional metals that deform permanently when bent, SMAs return to their pre-set shape when warmed above their transformation temperature. Nitinol is the most widely used SMA, with applications in medicine, engineering and consumer products.

Scale of production does not just affect cost — it can also change which metal is the most practical choice. At low volumes, a designer might specify aluminium plate machined from stock because no tooling investment is needed; at mass production volumes the same part might be die cast in aluminium alloy instead, because the excellent surface finish and dimensional accuracy of die casting eliminates secondary machining steps. Similarly, a one-off bespoke bracket might be fabricated from mild steel using basic hand tools, while the mass-produced equivalent would be press-formed from high-strength steel sheet to give a lighter, more consistent component at a fraction of the cost per unit.

glossary_terms.definition: A sustainability framework comprising six strategies: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Reclaim, Repair and Rethink; applied to assess and improve the environmental impact of a product across its lifecycle.
Metallic alloys that can return to a pre-defined shape when heated to a specific transformation temperature, even after being deformed; the most common example is nitinol (nickel-titanium).
Manufacturing a set number of identical products together before switching to a different product; tooling costs are shared across the batch, reducing unit cost compared to one-off production.
An economic model designed to keep materials in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling, eliminating waste and reducing reliance on finite raw material extraction.

practice_questions.text: Describe why recycling aluminium is significantly more sustainable than producing virgin aluminium from bauxite.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Recycling aluminium uses only approximately 5% of the energy required to smelt primary aluminium from bauxite ore.
• This greatly reduces CO₂ emissions associated with aluminium production, lowering its carbon footprint.
• Recycling also reduces the need for bauxite mining, which destroys habitats, pollutes waterways and generates significant quantities of toxic red mud waste as a by-product. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a nitinol stent is used to treat a blocked coronary artery.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Nitinol is a shape memory alloy with a transformation temperature set close to body temperature (37°C).
• The stent is cooled below its transformation temperature and compressed (crimped) onto a catheter so it takes up a small diameter, allowing it to be guided through the blood vessel.
• Once positioned inside the blocked artery, the stent is exposed to body temperature and recovers its pre-set expanded shape, opening the artery and holding it open.
• This approach eliminates the need for a mechanical inflation device (balloon), reducing the complexity of the procedure and the risk of damage to the artery wall.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how applying the 6Rs framework to a steel garden gate can reduce its environmental impact across its full lifecycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reduce: design the gate using less steel (e.g. hollow tube section rather than solid bar) to reduce embodied energy without compromising structural performance.
Reuse: if the gate is removed during renovation, it can be sold or donated for reuse at another property, avoiding the energy cost of remanufacture.
Recycle: at end of life, the steel can be 100% recycled; recycled steel uses approximately 74% less energy than virgin steel, significantly reducing lifecycle carbon.
Reclaim: steel swarf from machining gate components is reclaimed by the fabricator and returned to a scrap dealer or smelter.
Repair: rather than replacing a corroded gate, sandblasting and re-painting or re-galvanising extends its life, deferring replacement and the associated resource consumption.
Rethink: designing the gate without mixed-material components (e.g. plastic decorative elements bonded to steel) makes end-of-life recycling easier and more effective.
[6 marks — Mastering: At least four of the 6Rs applied specifically to the steel gate with developed environmental impact explanation. Secure: Three Rs applied with some development. Developing: Two Rs listed with limited development; little link to environmental impact. Emerging: Vague mention of recycling without development.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using batch production compared to mass production for manufacturing cast iron garden furniture.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of batch production for cast iron garden furniture:
• Lower initial capital investment; sand casting equipment and tooling is cheaper than the automated lines and dies required for mass production, making it accessible to small and medium manufacturers.
• Flexibility to switch between furniture designs between batches; allows the manufacturer to offer a range of styles and update designs in response to changing consumer preferences.
• Batch production is well suited to seasonal demand for garden furniture; stock can be built up in winter and sold in spring/summer without maintaining year-round continuous production.
• Sand casting, typical of batch production for cast iron, can produce complex decorative forms (scroll work, botanical motifs) that reflect the aesthetic value of traditional cast iron furniture.
Disadvantages of batch production compared to mass production:
• Higher unit cost than mass production because tooling investment is spread over a smaller number of units, and manual processes require more labour per item.
• Longer setup time between batches as moulds are prepared and tooling changed; this reduces overall production efficiency.
• Greater variability in component quality compared to highly automated mass production; sand casting requires more post-casting finishing (grinding, shot blasting).
• Mass production would produce each item far more quickly and at lower unit cost if demand justified it, with tighter dimensional consistency.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion of at least two developed advantages and two disadvantages of batch vs mass production, linked to cast iron furniture context (tooling cost, flexibility, quality, unit cost). Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; poor balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]
